claims.text: There are definitely more than two options to ensure people in Costa Rica are okay with whoever wins the upcoming election.
The president almost never has actual complete power of the country.
If a candidate wins that people are nervous about, they should turn to their elected officials to represent and defend them from possible harms.
We must always be wary and be sure to protect the rights of all human beings, especially those in the LGBTQI community.

implicit_assumptions: There exists a mechanism by which elected officials can protect citizens if they feel threatened.
The government’s power is constrained by other branches or institutions.
LGBTQI rights are a concern that warrants special protection.
decomposition.reasoning_relation: premises support the conclusion via an argument of practical precaution.
scope_notes: The claim that options exist is presented as definite: 'definitely' implies certainty.
Warnings about the president’s limited power are framed as general truth, implying a broad scope across all future presidents.
The recommendation to engage elected officials is conditional on citizen nervousness, indicating a contingent scope.
uncertainty: The statement about ‘definitely more than two options’ is assertive but not empirically checked.
The claim regarding the president’s power relies on unstated constitutional knowledge.

Inference.supporting_quote: There are definitely more than two options to ensure people in Costa Rica are okay with whoever wins the upcoming election.
Inference.structure_objection: The premises talk about the limited power of the president and citizens turning to elected officials, but they do not establish that there are more than two distinct ways to secure citizen comfort. The claim of a definite set of options lacks empirical support
Inference.alternative_interpretation: A more cautious claim—'there are potentially multiple ways'—would be justified by the premises.
